This cluster of papers focuses on the classification, molecular profiling, genetic pathogenesis, and treatment strategies for various types of lymphoid neoplasms, including Hodgkin's lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, and peripheral T-cell lymphoma. It also explores the use of PET imaging, rituximab therapy, and gene expression profiling to predict survival and guide treatment decisions.

A colleague from another field brings you this problem:

A reinforcement-learning agent learns to control a simulated physical
system on a hexagonal grid. Learning works but needs tens of millions of
environment steps; the simulator is the bottleneck. Standard tricks tried:
frame skipping, prioritised replay, reward shaping, curriculum. Want a
different angle on sample efficiency.

Look at it the way your field would. Propose an approach that draws on what you know.
proposal:
# A pathologist's-eye view on this

My day job is deciding, from a small, expensive tissue sample, what a much larger and more expensive process (a patient's disease trajectory) is going to do — and then deciding what to do about it before we can afford to wait and see. That's structurally the same problem your colleague has: an expensive "ground truth" process (the simulator, in your case; the natural history of the lymphoma, in mine) and a need to make good decisions with far fewer expensive observations than brute force would require. Oncology built an entire methodological toolkit around exactly this bottleneck. Here's how I'd map it onto your RL problem.

## The core analogy

| Lymphoma field concept | What it actually solves | RL analogue |
|---|---|---|
| **Surrogate endpoints** (progression-free survival used instead of overall survival in trials) | Waiting for the "true" outcome (death, years later) is too slow/expensive to power a trial — so we validate a cheaper, earlier-available signal that correlates with the true outcome and use *that* to make decisions | A learned world-model / cheap surrogate simulator, validated against the real simulator, used for the bulk of rollouts |
| **International Prognostic Index (IPI)** — 5 crude clinical variables (age, stage, LDH, performance status, extranodal sites) that stratify risk almost as well as full genomic profiling | Compresses a huge, expensive feature space (genomics) into a small sufficient statistic for the decision that matters (risk/treatment choice) | State abstraction: learn a low-dimensional "prognostic" embedding of the environment state that's sufficient for value estimation, so you don't need to relearn value from scratch for every superficially-different state |
| **Interim PET-adapted therapy** (Hodgkin/DLBCL: scan after 2 cycles, escalate or de-escalate before the full course is done) | Uses an early, cheap partial read to decide whether continuing the expensive full course is worth it | Short-horizon bootstrapped value estimates / learned "is this trajectory worth finishing" critic — truncate or redirect expensive simulator rollouts early |
| **Cell-of-origin / molecular subtyping** (GCB vs ABC DLBCL via gene expression) | Clusters a heterogeneous population into subtypes that share prognosis and treatment response, so evidence from one patient generalizes to others in the same subtype | Unsupervised clustering of visited states/episodes into "subtypes"; share/generalize value and policy updates within a cluster instead of treating every state as novel |
| **Bayesian adaptive trial design / continual reassessment method** (dose-finding trials that update assignment probabilities as data accrues, to minimize patients exposed to a bad dose) | Chooses the *next* expensive observation to maximize information gained, rather than sampling uniformly | Active/Bayesian selection of which trajectories to actually run on the real simulator — spend expensive steps where model uncertainty or policy uncertainty is highest |
| **Multi-center trial pooling / meta-analysis** | Pools smaller cohorts across sites so each site needs fewer patients to reach a powered conclusion | Multi-task/transfer RL across procedurally varied instances of the environment, pooling experience rather than training each variant from scratch |

## The concrete proposal

Put together, this isn't just "use a world model" — it's a specific discipline for *how much to trust it and when to check it*, borrowed from how we validate and deploy surrogate endpoints in practice:

1. **Build the surrogate.** Train a learned dynamics/reward model of the hex-grid environment from the real simulator data already being generated. This is your "surrogate endpoint" — cheap, available immediately, imperfect.

2. **Validate it like a surrogate endpoint, not just an ML model.** In oncology, a surrogate isn't accepted just because it's correlated with outcome at the population level (Prentice's criteria) — it has to capture the *full effect* of the intervention on the outcome, or it can mislead you into thinking a treatment works when it doesn't. Same trap here: check that the surrogate simulator's *ranking of policies/actions* matches the real simulator's, not just that its one-step predictions look accurate. A model that predicts states well but gets long-horizon credit assignment wrong is a surrogate that "looks validated" and isn't — exactly the failure mode that has burned drug trials that leaned on weak surrogates.

3. **Do the bulk of training against the surrogate (Dyna-style), reserving real simulator steps as the expensive "confirmatory" resource** — the RL equivalent of running a phase III trial only after the surrogate-guided phase II has narrowed the field.

4. **Spend the real-simulator budget where you're most uncertain, not uniformly.** Use something like a continual-reassessment-method logic: track surrogate-vs-real disagreement (or policy-value uncertainty) online, and preferentially route real rollouts to the states/trajectories where that disagreement is highest — this is where the marginal real step buys the most information, same logic as adaptive dose-finding minimizing wasted patient exposure to uninformative doses.

5. **Learn a compact "IPI-style" state abstraction alongside this.** Rather than let the world model and value function operate on raw high-dimensional hex-grid state, learn (or hand-engineer, then verify by ablation) a small set of features that are sufficient for the value function — the equivalent of showing that 5 clinical variables get you 90% of what full genomic sequencing gets you. This directly attacks sample efficiency because it shrinks the effective space the agent has to cover.

6. **Cluster episodes into "subtypes" and share credit within cluster** — analogous to cell-of-origin subtyping. If many superficially different starting configurations on the hex grid actually behave the same way dynamically, detecting that clustering (e.g., via a learned embedding + unsupervised clustering, checked against whether value/policy actually transfers within cluster) lets experience in one member of a cluster update belief about the whole cluster, rather than being wasted as a one-off.

The throughline from my field: **don't try to make the expensive process cheaper directly — build a validated cheap proxy for it, spend the expensive process's budget only where the proxy is least trustworthy, and compress the state space down to whatever small set of variables actually drives outcome.** That's a different axis than frame-skipping/prioritized-replay/reward-shaping/curriculum, which all still assume you're paying for every unit of real simulator time; this instead asks how little of that expensive resource you can get away with paying for at all.
